missing_spec_content.spec_text: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never mentions the LDR or how its resistance depends on light intensity. The spec also lists LDRs among components whose 'resistance ... is not constant'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The application of LDRs in circuits eg switching lights on when it gets dark is required.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives no LDR application.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The applications of thermistors in circuits eg a thermostat is required.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says a thermistor's resistance falls as it gets hotter. It gives no application, such as a thermostat.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: draw an appropriate circuit diagram using correct circuit symbols.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson describes the circuit only in words. It does not teach circuit symbols or how to draw the circuit diagram.

missing_spec_content.spec_text:
energy transferred = power × time

E = P t
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson teaches E = QV only. E = Pt, which students must recall and apply, is missing.

missing_spec_content.spec_text:
Students should be able to explain how the power of a circuit device is related to:

- the potential difference across it and the current through it
- the energy transferred over a given time.
missing_spec_content.why: Power is not covered anywhere in the lesson.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe how different domestic appliances transfer energy from batteries or ac mains to the kinetic energy of electric motors or the energy of heating devices.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not describe energy transfers in everyday appliances. The intro only mentions a phone, a kettle and Christmas lights in passing.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe, with examples, the relationship between the power ratings for domestic electrical appliances and the changes in stored energy when they are in use.
Work is done when charge flows in a circuit.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson talks about energy transferred per coulomb. It never states that work is done when charge flows, or that energy is transferred by electrical work.

above_gcse.text: Conventional current goes the opposite way, from positive to negative. This is just a historical habit. Scientists chose the direction before they discovered electrons, and got it the wrong way round.
above_gcse.why: The specification sections given do not mention conventional current or electron flow direction. The lesson presents it as a frequent exam trap (tutor_note: 'catch people out every year'), which may make the student over-focus on content these sections do not require.

above_gcse.text: Ampere (A) — the unit of current. 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹
above_gcse.why: Negative-index unit notation (C s⁻¹, and V A⁻¹ in keyPoints[2].keyTerms[1]) is not used in the specification and may confuse a 15-year-old. 'Coulombs per second' is enough.

factual_errors.text: Two factors affect resistance: - length: resistance increases with the length of the wire - temperature
factual_errors.correction: Length and temperature are not the only factors that affect resistance. For example, the resistance of an LDR depends on light intensity. Cross-sectional area and material also affect a wire's resistance. The text should say 'Two factors you need here include…' or similar.

factual_errors.text: A component whose resistance stays constant — gives a straight-line I-V graph
factual_errors.correction: An ohmic conductor's resistance is constant only at constant temperature. The current through it is then directly proportional to the potential difference.

wrong_terms.text: Current and voltage — the basics of every circuit
Current, voltage and resistance let you predict exactly how any circuit will behave.

not_checked: Every keyPoints[].diagram is null. No I-V graph sketches or circuit diagrams could be checked. The graph shapes (for example 'Curve that bends away from straight line (S-shape)' in tables[0]) were judged from the text alone.
The examTip claim 'Questions using Q = It, E = QV and R = V/I come up almost every year' could not be checked against past papers.
The skills details referred to in the spec ('page 91', 'page 93') were not supplied. Lesson coverage of WS/MS/AT skills could not be checked.
